title: Area III review: Airport and Seaplane Base Operations
intro: These questions mix both Tasks of Area III: radio calls, light signals and airport lighting, plus traffic patterns. Most put you in one commercial flight where you need both Tasks at once, from charter departures to no-radio arrivals.

questions.q: You arrive at night at Ridgeview just after its part-time tower has closed. The sectional shows a star by the tower frequency and "RP 23" in the airport data. You will land on Runway 23. What is your plan for the radio, the lights and the pattern?
options: Call the tower frequency and ask the controller to turn the runway lights up
Self-announce on the CTAF, key the lighting frequency from the Chart Supplement 7 times, and fly right traffic for Runway 23
Fly left traffic, because RP notes apply only while the tower is open
Key the mike 3 times first so the lights don't blind you, and fly whichever pattern direction suits you
questions.why: With the tower closed and no FSS, you self-announce on the CTAF [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g2]]. Pilot-controlled lighting is often available when a part-time tower is closed [[33:129|AIM 2-1-8]]; key 7 times first for full intensity, then adjust down, and get the frequency from the Chart Supplement or approach chart, because it is not on the sectional [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8c-d]]. "RP 23" means a right pattern on Runway 23 [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1.1]]. The tempting "left traffic" answer is wrong: the 91.126 flow rules still apply when a towered airport is operating as a non-towered one [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1.1]], and right patterns are not charted at full-time towers, so this note is meant for exactly this time [[33:240|AIM 4-3-3d]]. Asking the tower fails because the tower controls the lights only while it is operating [[33:129|AIM 2-1-7]].

questions.q: On a 5-mile final at a non-towered airport, you are flying a practice RNAV approach to Runway 9 and plan to circle to Runway 27, which has right traffic. A Cessna is in the pattern. Which plan follows the guidance?
options: Announce "JAWBO inbound, RNAV 9" and circle to the left, since circling approaches always use left turns
Fly straight in to Runway 9 against the flow, since IFR traffic has priority
Announce your fix names on the CTAF so instrument pilots know where you are, then circle to the right
Announce "5 miles west, inbound RNAV Runway 9, circling Runway 27," coordinate with the Cessna, and circle to the right
questions.why: A non-instrument pilot may not know where your fixes are, so give direction and distance from the airport plus your intentions [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.5]] [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.11.5]]. Final for Runway 9 lies west of the airport, since you fly east to land. If the Chart Supplement lists right traffic, practice approaches in VMC circle to the right, and IFR traffic has no priority over VFR traffic [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.3]]. Coordinating with pattern traffic, breaking off to join downwind may be safest [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.4.2]]. The fix-name answer has the right turn direction but the wrong call.

questions.q: In daylight your radio dies just outside a Class D airport. The weather is VFR. You stay clear until you learn the traffic flow, join the pattern, and on final the tower gives you a steady green. The PAPI shows one white and three red. What now?
options: You are cleared to land; add power and pitch to get back to two white and two red, and stay at or above that glide path
Go around, because a no-radio airplane needs a flashing green before it may land
Continue as you are, since the glide path rule applies only to large and turbine-powered airplanes
Steady green means return for landing, so fly another pattern and wait for the next signal
questions.why: With a VFR radio failure you may land in Class D with basic VFR weather, visual contact with the tower and a clearance to land [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)(2)]], and a steady green in flight is that clearance [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. One white and three red is slightly low [[33:124|AIM FIG 2-1-5]]. In Class D any airplane landing on a runway with a visual approach slope indicator must stay at or above the glide path until lower is needed for a safe landing [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(e)(3)]]. The tempting "large and turbine only" answer mixes up paragraph (e)(1), the 1,500-foot entry rule, with (e)(3), which covers every airplane. Flashing green, not steady green, means return for landing [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

questions.q: You fly a single-engine turboprop for a charter company out of a Class D airport at 640 feet MSL. No departure procedure or cloud clearance gets in the way. Which of these is a regulation for you there, not just a recommendation?
options: Fly the pattern at 1,640 feet MSL, the same as the piston traffic
Cross midfield at 2,640 feet MSL before an entry from the upwind side
After takeoff, climb to 2,140 feet MSL as rapidly as practicable
Leave the pattern with a 45 degree turn after reaching pattern altitude
questions.why: In Class D, each pilot of a turbine-powered airplane must climb to 1,500 feet above the surface as rapidly as practicable [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(g)(2)]]: 640 + 1,500 = 2,140 feet MSL. You must also enter the pattern at least 1,500 feet above the airport (2,140 feet MSL), so 1,640 feet MSL is too low for you [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(e)(1)]]. The 2,000-foot AGL midfield crossing (640 + 2,000 = 2,640) is AFH advice for pilots at airports where turbine aircraft operate, not a rule [[24:168|AFH 8-4]], and the 45 degree departure turn is a recommended practice [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.8]].

questions.q: Approach is giving you VFR traffic advisories. A strong wind from your left has you holding a big crab to the left to stay on course. Approach calls traffic at 12 o'clock, 3 miles, opposite direction. Where should you look first?
options: Exactly where the nose points, since the clock position is based on your heading
Somewhat left of the nose, toward the wind
Somewhat right of the nose, since the clock position is based on your track
Behind you, since opposite-direction traffic passes on the left
questions.why: Radar shows the controller your track, not your heading, so when you hold a wind correction the traffic will appear off to one side of the issued position [[33:216|AIM 4-1-15d]]. Application: crabbed left, your nose points left of your track, so traffic straight ahead on your track sits to the right of the nose. Looking where the nose points assumes ATC can see your heading, which it cannot. Keep scanning anyway: advisories don't relieve you of see and avoid [[33:214|AIM 4-1-15]].

questions.q: Ten miles north of Lakeview, a non-towered airport, you are about to make your first CTAF call. Runway 27 is in use with left traffic, and a Cirrus is already on downwind. Which call follows the AIM and AC 90-66C?
options: "Lakeview traffic, Bonanza Four Kilo X-ray, ten miles north, three thousand five hundred, inbound, will enter left downwind Runway Two Seven, full stop, Lakeview"
"Lakeview traffic, Bonanza Four Kilo X-ray, ten miles north, three thousand five hundred, will enter left downwind Runway Two Seven, number two behind the Cirrus, Lakeview"
"Lakeview traffic, Bonanza Four Kilo X-ray, ten miles north, three thousand five hundred, entering left downwind for the active, Lakeview"
"Bonanza Four Kilo X-ray, ten miles north, descending to two thousand, Runway Two Seven"
questions.why: Self-announce your position, altitude and intentions about 10 miles out [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.1]], say the airport name at the start and the end, and name the runway number, never "active runway" [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g8]]. Don't broadcast your own landing sequence; that is ATC's job at towered airports [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.1]]. Avoid "to" and "for," which can be confused with runway numbers or altitudes [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.3]]. The "number two" call sounds helpful but announces a sequence, and the call with no airport name also uses "to."

questions.q: No radio, you are on final at a towered airport when the tower shines a flashing red light at you. What does it mean?
options: Give way to other aircraft and keep circling
Taxi clear of the runway in use
Return for landing; a steady green will follow
The airport is unsafe; do not land
questions.why: In flight, flashing red means the airport is unsafe, do not land [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. So go around and keep visual contact with the tower for further signals [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a3]]. "Taxi clear of the runway in use" is the same signal's meaning for an aircraft on the surface, the most common mix-up. Steady red means give way and keep circling, and flashing green means return for landing [[33:257|AIM TBL 4-3-1]].

questions.q: You land behind a business jet that touched down about 1,200 feet beyond the displaced threshold of Runway 27. The displaced area in front of the threshold bar is 900 feet long. Where should you plan to touch down?
options: In the displaced area, to get the most runway ahead of you
Beyond the point where the jet touched down
Just past the threshold bar, well before the jet's touchdown point
Anywhere past the threshold bar, since the jet's wake ended when it slowed down
questions.why: Landing behind a larger aircraft on the same runway, stay at or above its final approach path, note its touchdown point and land beyond it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b1]], because its wake ends at touchdown [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4a]]. The displaced area is available for takeoffs either way and landings only from the opposite direction, so you may not land there on Runway 27 [[33:141|AIM 2-3-3h2]]. Landing short of the jet's touchdown point puts you in the wake it left on final.

questions.q: You are taxiing out at an airport with Runway Status Lights. To keep the ground radar screen clear, your passenger suggests leaving the transponder in STBY until you take the runway, as "Lights, Camera, Action" says. What is right?
options: Turn on altitude reporting and ADS-B Out when you leave parking, and leave them on until you shut down at parking
Leave it in STBY until cleared for takeoff, then turn it on
Turn it on only if the tower asks you to squawk
Leave it in STBY on the ground; RWSL works from the tower's clearances, not from your transponder
questions.why: At RWSL airports, operate with the transponder and ADS-B on from leaving the parking area until shutdown at parking, so the surveillance systems that drive RWSL can see you [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6d1]]. At all airports, use altitude reporting and ADS-B Out anywhere on the movement area [[33:221|AIM 4-1-20a3]]. "Lights, Camera, Action" is a final check when cleared for takeoff or before taking the runway, not the first time to turn the transponder on [[16:10|AC 90-48E 10.4.1]]. RWSL is fully automatic and works from surveillance data, not clearances [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6a]].

questions.q: On a charter flight, a passenger becomes ill and needs a doctor soon, but is stable, and the airplane is fine. You are talking to Approach on an assigned code, 30 miles from a towered airport. What is the best call?
options: "MAYDAY" three times, then squawk 7700
Squawk 7700 first, then call on 121.5
"PAN-PAN" three times, then your call sign, the problem and your intentions, keeping your assigned code
Wait until you reach the tower, since a sick passenger is not an emergency
questions.why: This is an urgency condition: a safety concern needing timely help. Use PAN-PAN, preferably three times; it has priority over all communications except distress [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1c-d]]. In contact with ATC, keep your assigned code; 7700 is for when you can't make contact right away [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]]. Then give the message elements in order [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a3]]. MAYDAY is for grave and imminent danger. Waiting is the classic error: ask for help early, not after it becomes distress [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2a]].

questions.q: You are holding short of Runway 27 when the tower says, "Bonanza Four Kilo X-ray, Runway 27, cleared for takeoff, caution wake turbulence, departing Citation." The wind is 120 at 4. Where should you plan to lift off, and what about the wind?
options: Beyond the Citation's lift-off point, since its wake ends there
Anywhere, because a crosswind of 1 to 5 knots blows the wake off the runway
Wait at least 2 minutes, since a departing jet always requires it
Before the Citation's rotation point, then climb above its path; the light quartering tailwind needs maximum caution
questions.why: Departing behind a larger aircraft, note its rotation point, rotate before it, and climb above its path until you turn clear [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b6]]. Wake begins at rotation [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4a]]. Wind 120 on Runway 27 is 150 degrees off the runway heading, a light quartering tailwind, and the AIM says the light quartering tailwind requires maximum caution because it can move vortices forward into your path [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4b]]. A light crosswind can hold the upwind vortex on the runway, not blow it away [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4b]]. The 2-minute wait is for a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b8]].

questions.q: On short final behind a business jet, you hit its wake. The airplane rolls, and a wingtip scrapes the runway as you land. No one is hurt, and only the wingtip is damaged. What does 49 CFR 830 require, and what was the wake lesson?
options: Notify the NTSB immediately, because any wake upset counts as a flight control system malfunction
No NTSB notice is required, since wingtip damage is not substantial damage and no listed serious incident occurred; next time stay at or above the jet's path and land beyond its touchdown point
File an NTSB report within 10 days, because any damage to the aircraft makes it an accident
No NTSB notice is required; next time land before the jet's touchdown point
questions.why: An accident needs death, serious injury or substantial damage [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]]. Damage to wingtips is specifically not substantial damage [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]]. A wake upset is not on the immediate-notice list of serious incidents, which covers things like a flight control system malfunction or failure, an in-flight fire or an in-flight collision [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5(a)]]. The controls worked, so the malfunction answer is wrong. To avoid the wake, stay at or above the larger aircraft's path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b1]].

questions.q: At a towered airport, the tower says, "Bonanza Four Kilo X-ray, follow the Citation on a 3-mile final, Runway 27, cleared to land." You have the Citation in sight. What is the best reply, and who handles the spacing?
options: "Roger, Four Kilo X-ray." ATC keeps you clear of the Citation's wake
"Cleared to land, Four Kilo X-ray." Land before the Citation's touchdown point to stay below its wake
"Cleared to land Runway 27, Bonanza Four Kilo X-ray." You now take responsibility for safe spacing and wake avoidance
"Cleared to land Runway 27, Bonanza Four Kilo X-ray." ATC stays responsible for wake separation because it told you to follow
questions.why: Your initial readback of a landing clearance should include the runway [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7b4]]. Accepting an instruction to follow an aircraft means you will ensure safe landing intervals and accept responsibility for wake turbulence separation [[34:153|AIM 7-4-8b]]. So stay at or above the Citation's path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b1]]. The answer that keeps ATC responsible for the wake has the right readback but gets the responsibility backward.

questions.q: Ready at the hold line of Runway 27, you hear, "Bonanza Four Kilo X-ray, Runway 27, line up and wait." What do you do?
options: Read back "Runway 27, line up and wait, Bonanza Four Kilo X-ray," scan final and the runway, then line up and wait for a takeoff clearance
Say "Roger, Four Kilo X-ray" and taxi onto the runway
Read it back, then start the takeoff roll once you are aligned
Read it back, and turn the transponder on only when you are cleared for takeoff
questions.why: Always read back a runway assignment and any instruction to hold short or line up and wait [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18a9]]. When cleared to line up and wait, scan the final approach and look down the runway before entering it, and check that you are on the right runway [[16:10|AC 90-48E 10.4.1]]. Line up and wait is not a takeoff clearance; you need a clearance to take off [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(i)]]. "Roger" only means you received the transmission [[34:407|AIM P/C Glossary]]. The transponder should already be in altitude reporting mode on the movement area [[33:221|AIM 4-1-20a3]].

questions.q: In VMC at a non-towered airport, you are passing 400 feet AGL on final and the PAPI shows four white. To land in the touchdown zone you would need about 1,300 feet per minute down. What should you do?
options: Push over to 1,300 feet per minute, since being above the glide path is always legal
Go around, since you were not stabilized by 500 feet above the airport
Make a 360 on final to lose height, then land
Continue at the normal descent rate and land long, wherever you touch down
questions.why: Four white means high, more than 3.5 degrees [[33:124|AIM FIG 2-1-5]]. Pilots typically go around if not stabilized by 500 feet above the airport in VMC, and a stabilized approach has a descent rate of generally 500 to 1,000 feet per minute, cut back before 300 feet AGL if over 500 [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Staying above the glide path is what the Class D VASI rule asks [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(e)(3)]], but being legal doesn't make a 1,300 foot per minute dive at 400 feet stable. A 360 on final would cut across the pattern flow; at a tower you'd never make one without first telling the controller, unless asked or in an emergency [[33:244|AIM 4-3-5]] [[33:245|AIM 4-3-5]].

questions.q: IFR in a complex single, your radios fail in VMC 30 miles from your destination, a Class D airport where the weather is good VFR. What is the best plan?
options: Keep flying the 91.185(c) route and altitude and start the approach at your ETA
Land at the nearest strip you can reach, even a short one, because "practicable" means "possible"
Fly straight in, since an IFR flight plan doesn't need a landing clearance after a radio failure
Continue VFR and land as soon as practicable: squawk 7600, stay outside or above the Class D surface area until you know the traffic flow, join the pattern and land on a steady green
questions.why: If the failure occurs in VFR conditions, continue under VFR and land as soon as practicable [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(b)]]. "Practicable" is not "possible": you don't have to use an unsuitable airport or land minutes short of your destination [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1c2]]. Squawk 7600 [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]], then follow the no-radio arrival: remain outside or above the surface area until you know the flow, join the pattern and watch for light signals [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a3]]. Landing in Class D still needs a clearance, which can be a steady green [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)(2)]] [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. The 91.185(c) route and altitude are for failures in IFR conditions.

questions.q: No radio information is available as you overfly a non-towered airport with Runways 9 and 27. The wind sock hangs limp. The small end of the tetrahedron points west, and the traffic pattern indicators show right traffic for Runway 27. You hear and see no other traffic. What is the best plan?
options: Runway 27 is indicated, but treat the tetrahedron with extreme caution in calm wind; if you use 27, fly right traffic as the indicators show
Land Runway 9, because the small end of the tetrahedron points into the wind
Land Runway 27 with left traffic, since left turns are always standard
Skip the pattern and fly a straight-in, since no one is around
questions.why: The small end of a tetrahedron points in the direction of landing, so pointing west means Runway 27. In very light or calm wind, use extreme caution, because it may not match the calm-wind runway [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4b3]]. When approaching to land, all turns are to the left unless a traffic pattern indicator shows right turns [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4c]] [[60:451|14 CFR 91.126(b)]]. Check the indicators from above pattern altitude, then fly well clear before descending to enter [[17:14|AC 90-66C 11.2]]. Some aircraft have no radio, so silence doesn't mean an empty pattern [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.12.2]], and the FAA discourages VFR straight-ins [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g4]].

questions.q: At night on a 2-mile final to a Class D airport, the pulsating VASI changes from steady red to pulsing red. What is happening, and what do you do?
options: You are slightly low; ease the nose up without adding power
You are well below the glide path; retract some flaps to gain lift
You are getting further below the glide path; add power and raise the nose together until you see the on-path signal, then stay at or above it
You are above the glide path; reduce power
questions.why: Steady red is slightly below the glide path; pulsing red means you have descended further below it. On path is steady white or alternating red and white [[33:125|AIM 2-1-2d]]. In Class D you must stay at or above the glide path until lower is needed for a safe landing [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(e)(3)]]. When low, add power and raise the nose together [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. Pitch alone causes a high sink rate or a low-altitude stall [[24:175|AFH 9-4]], and retracting flaps for an undershoot can cause a sudden loss of lift and excessive sink [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Pulsing white, not red, means above the glide path.

questions.q: On the tower frequency you hear another pilot say, "Tower, Mooney Two Three Papa, ten south, landing, with the numbers." The airport has ATIS. What has that pilot told the tower?
options: That he has the current ATIS, so the controller can skip everything in it
That he has the ATIS and the weather from the ASOS
That he has the runway assignment and is cleared to land
Only that he has the wind, runway and altimeter, not the ATIS
questions.why: "Have numbers" means you have received the wind, runway and altimeter ONLY. It does not mean you have the ATIS and should never be used for that [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13h]]. The right way is to repeat the ATIS code letter on initial contact, such as "information Sierra received" [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13d]]. Then the controller may omit current items in the broadcast [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13e]]. Without the code, the controller has to give that pilot the pertinent information [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13f]]. Nothing in the call is a landing clearance; you still need one from the tower [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(i)]].

questions.q: After a night landing you exit on a taxiway whose centerline lights alternate green and yellow. The tower tells you to contact Ground. Where may you stop?
options: As soon as the airplane is off the runway pavement
Only after you pass the alternating green and yellow lights, since until then you are still within the runway environment or ILS critical area
At the first yellow light, which marks the hold line
Anywhere on the taxiway, since green and yellow lights are only for low visibility
questions.why: Lead-off lights alternate green and yellow from the runway centerline to one light beyond the runway holding position or ILS critical area holding position. The color code warns you that you are still within the runway environment or ILS critical area [[33:126|AIM 2-1-5c]]. Being off the pavement edge is not the same as being clear. Taxiway centerline lights beyond that point are steady green [[33:133|AIM 2-1-10b]].

questions.q: In daylight your radio quits on the ramp at a towered airport. You phone the tower and get approval to depart without two-way radio. At the hold line you get a steady green. How do you acknowledge, and what does it mean?
options: Rock your wings; it means cleared to taxi onto the runway and hold
Blink the landing light; it means return to the starting point
Move the ailerons or rudder; it means cleared for takeoff
Move the ailerons or rudder; it means cleared to taxi
questions.why: If the radio fails before you leave parking and can't be fixed, phone the tower for authorization to depart without two-way radio. On the ground in daylight, acknowledge light signals by moving the ailerons or rudder [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13b]]. A steady green to an aircraft on the surface means cleared for takeoff; flashing green means cleared to taxi, and flashing white means return to starting point [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. Rocking the wings is the in-flight acknowledgment [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a2]].
